title: Seizing on arrival after a mixed sedative overdose

source.citation: Giwa A, Oey E. The return of an old nemesis: Survival after severe tricyclic antidepressant toxicity, a case report. Toxicol Rep. 2018;5:357-362.

presentation.chiefComplaint: Generalized seizure after an intentional overdose
presentation.hpi: Brought in by EMS about 2–3 hours after an apparently intentional overdose of an unknown quantity of alprazolam, eszopiclone and tramadol. She had recently been voicing suicidal thoughts and has attempted suicide before. She is having a generalized tonic–clonic seizure on the EMS stretcher as she arrives. Asked about any other medication she could have taken, her partner at first says there is none.
meds: Regular medications not documented; the overdose involved alprazolam, eszopiclone and tramadol
presentation.social: Recent suicidal ideation, reported by EMS and her partner.

exam: Generalized tonic–clonic seizure on arrival, stopping immediately after lorazepam 2 mg IV
After the seizure: GCS 8, so intubation is prepared to protect the airway; SpO2 99% on a non-rebreather mask
Over the first 2 h on telemetry: repeated widening of the QRS, each episode followed by pulseless ventricular tachycardia (five arrests)
After the fifth return of circulation (about 2.5 h after arrival): further seizure activity

investigations.name: Urine drug screen
investigations.value: Benzodiazepines positive; amphetamines, barbiturates, cocaine, opiates, PCP, methadone and cannabinoids negative

investigations.name: EEG
investigations.value: No intracranial cause of the seizures

imaging.finding: No structural or ischemic cause of the cardiac arrests
No intracranial cause of the seizures

ecg: Wide-complex tachycardia, ventricular rate 165/min, QRS > 150 ms (read as possible polymorphic VT). After one ampule of sodium bicarbonate: regular tachycardia 153/min, QRS narrowed to 156 ms, QTc 619 ms.

diagnosis.primary: Nortriptyline poisoning (undisclosed tricyclic co-ingestion) with seizures, wide-complex tachycardia and recurrent pulseless ventricular tachycardia
differentials: Structural heart disease with ventricular tachycardia

management: Lorazepam 2 mg IV for the seizure
Sodium bicarbonate 8.4% 50 mEq IV and a 2 L normal saline bolus: partial narrowing of the QRS
Rapid sequence intubation (etomidate, rocuronium); propofol and fentanyl infusions
Second bicarbonate ampule after intubation, then a sodium bicarbonate infusion
Five pulseless VT arrests within 2 h: CPR, defibrillation, repeated sodium bicarbonate boluses and epinephrine, plus magnesium 2 g and calcium; ROSC after each
Amiodarone 300 mg and infusion at the fifth arrest; stopped within 3 h after cardiology review
Levetiracetam and propofol for recurrent seizures
Activated charcoal via nasogastric tube once the rhythm was stable
ICU admission for targeted temperature management
outcome: Extubated after several days of targeted temperature management; no structural cardiac or intracranial cause found. Discharged 5 days after the arrests with normal neurological function and a narrow QRS (100 ms).
teachingPoints: Seizures, hyperthermia, tachycardia, a wide QRS and acidosis after an overdose point to a sodium-channel blocker such as a tricyclic, even when the history denies one: ask specifically.
A QRS above 100 ms predicts seizures and above 160 ms ventricular arrhythmias (Boehnert and Lovejoy); a terminal R wave in aVR is another marker.
Hypertonic sodium bicarbonate boluses (1–2 mEq/kg, repeated) are first line for QRS widening, hypotension and ventricular arrhythmias; alkalinization drives potassium down, so monitor and replace it.
Around intubation, give bicarbonate and keep minute ventilation high: respiratory acidosis worsens sodium-channel blockade.
For arrhythmias refractory to bicarbonate, lidocaine is preferred; avoid class IA and IC antiarrhythmics, and avoid flumazenil and physostigmine in tricyclic poisoning.

questions.q: Which agent best explains this presentation?
questions.extra: ECG: wide-complex tachycardia, rate 165/min, QRS > 150 ms. VBG: pH 6.94, pCO2 74 mm Hg, HCO3⁻ 16 mmol/L, K⁺ 3.8 mmol/L, lactate > 15 mmol/L.
questions.explanation: Seizures, hyperthermia, tachycardia, a QRS above 150 ms and severe acidosis are the sodium-channel blockade picture of tricyclic poisoning. Tramadol causes seizures but rarely this degree of QRS widening, and sedative-hypnotics cause neither. When asked again, her partner recalled a bottle of nortriptyline at home.

questions.q: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
questions.extra: ECG: wide-complex tachycardia, rate 165/min, QRS > 150 ms. BP 139/77 mm Hg; she has a pulse.
questions.explanation: Hypertonic sodium bicarbonate counters fast sodium-channel blockade through the sodium load and alkalinization; her QRS narrowed within minutes. Procainamide (class IA) deepens the block and is contraindicated, cardioversion rarely helps a toxin-induced wide-complex rhythm with a pulse, and amiodarone is not first line.

questions.q: Despite repeated bicarbonate boluses and an infusion, she has had two more pulseless VT arrests. Which antiarrhythmic is preferred?
questions.explanation: Lidocaine (class IB) binds and leaves sodium channels quickly and may displace the slowly dissociating tricyclic. Class IA and IC drugs deepen sodium-channel blockade and beta-blockers worsen hypotension. Amiodarone, given at her fifth arrest, is generally avoided because it prolongs the QT and adds sodium-channel and beta-blocking effects.

questions.q: Which treatment should be avoided in this patient?
questions.extra: Urine drug screen: benzodiazepines positive, opiates negative. Serum nortriptyline 1581 ng/mL (therapeutic 50–150).
options: Activated charcoal via a nasogastric tube
questions.explanation: Flumazenil can precipitate seizures and arrhythmias when a proconvulsant such as a tricyclic has been co-ingested, and is contraindicated here; physostigmine is likewise contraindicated in tricyclic poisoning. Charcoal through a protected airway, anticonvulsants after benzodiazepines and vasopressors for hypotension are all reasonable.

evidence.quote: A 34 year-old female with a past medical history of depression, anxiety, hypertension, and rheumatoid arthritis was brought in by emergency medical services (EMS)
brought in by Emergency Medical Services (EMS) with generalized tonic clonic seizure, status post intentional ingestion of multiple drugs
after taking an unknown quantity of alprazolam, eszopiclone, and tramadol in an apparent intentional overdose
she had been expressing some suicidal ideations, and had a previous history of attempted suicide
She was noted to be actively seizing (generalized tonic clonic) on the EMS stretcher upon arrival to the ED and was immediately given lorazepam 2 mg intravenously (IV)
As our patient was 2–3 h after ingestion
We asked the patient's significant other for any possible additional medications that she could have ingested, and after initially denying
he recalled she had an "unopened" bottle of nortriptyline that had been lying in a cabinet for several weeks
was noted to have a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) of 8. We prepared to protect her airway via endotracheal intubation
Temp 38.8 °C, heart rate (HR) 140 beats per minute, respiratory rate (RR) 25 breaths per minute
blood pressure (BP) 139/77 mmHg, oxygen saturation (SaO2) 99% on a nonrebreather facemask
with a total of 5 pulseless ventricular tachycardia arrests in the span of 2 h, each preceded by her cardiac telemetry showing a widened rhythm
Fifth ROSC. Myoclonic seizure activity noted, propofol restarted.
Wide complex tachycardia, concerning for polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. Ventricular rate at 165 BPM, QRS duration prolonged >150 msec.
Narrowing of QRS intervals is seen, rhythm appears regular, tachycardic, ventricular rate at 153 bpm, QRS prolonged 156 msec, QTc prolonged 619 msec.
Her initial venous blood gas at this time was pH 6.94, pCO2 74 mmHg, HCO3 16 mmHg, K 3.8 mEq/L, with a lactate that was >15 mmol/L
Her venous blood gas after the first cardiac arrest revealed a pH of 7.35, pCO2 50 mmHg, HCO3 28 mmHg, K 2.9 mEq/L, lactate 6.5 mmol/L.

U-Amphetamine | Negative
Her TCA (Nortriptyline) level was 1581 ng/mL (Table 2), with a therapeutic range of 50–150 ng/mL
Both laboratory and echocardiography did not reveal any ischemic or structural related causes of her cardiac arrest.
magnetic resonance imaging and an electroencephalography did not reveal any intracranial causes of her seizures
She was immediately given an ampule of sodium bicarbonate (8.4%, 50 mEq) and 2 liters of normal saline 0.9% bolus.
A repeat EKG was obtained (Fig. 2), and showed some narrowing of her previously widened QRS.
Rapid sequence intubation (RSI) was performed on first attempt with etomidate and rocuronium, and she was maintained on IV infusions of propofol and fentanyl for sedation.
Post intubation, the patient was given another ampule of sodium bicarbonate, with a subsequent bicarbonate drip (containing 100mEq of sodium bicarbonate)
another ampule of sodium bicarbonate, 2 g of magnesium, and two ampules of epinephrine were given before obtaining return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC)
with more rounds of both epinephrine, sodium bicarbonate, and calcium before ROSC was regained
Each arrest was followed by further boluses of IV sodium bicarbonate ampules, epinephrine, and defibrillation with ROSC after each arrest.
Despite ROSC, her hypotension persisted, so peripheral norepinephrine was started with an appropriate response to her blood pressure.
During the final pulseless ventricular tachycardic arrest, 300 mg of amiodarone was administered with a subsequent amiodarone drip.
the amiodarone drip was eventually discontinued within 3 h in conjunction with a cardiology consultation
Just as the triple lumen central line was being placed, the patient began to seize, and thus the propofol was restarted. She was also given levetiracetam
An NGT was finally placed and activated charcoal was administered in conjunction with the poison control's updated recommendations.
transferred to the medical intensive care unit for further care and to initiate Targeted Temperature Management (hypothermia)
The patient was extubated after several days of Targeted Temperature Management and continued cardiovascular support.
After 5 days of further stabilization, the patient had a subsequent complete recovery with normal neurological function at discharge from the medical unit.
Normal sinus rhythm, mild tachycardia with a ventricular rate of 109 bpm. QRS duration 100 msec and normal.
